unitDescription.value: In this unit, students design a website for a local business such as a café, shop, tradesperson or service. Students investigate how businesses use websites to share information, attract customers and promote their products or services. They consider the needs of different users and explore website layout, navigation, colours, images and accessibility. Students create user stories, develop design ideas and produce wireframes before building a functional website using GitHub Codespaces and generative AI. They test their website, collect feedback and make improvements to their final design. The unit focuses on user experience, design thinking, evaluation and the responsible use of AI, rather than advanced programming.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: In Digital Technologies, students should have frequent opportunities for authentic learning by making key connections with other learning areas.

description.value: Students design and develop an AI-assisted website for a local business. They identify the target audience, create user stories and design criteria, and investigate the information customers need from the website. Students develop a site map, alternative design ideas, wireframes and a simple visual style guide before using generative AI within GitHub Codespaces to build a functional website prototype. They test the website with users, collect feedback and make improvements to the layout, navigation, accessibility and content. The final submission includes the design work, working website prototype, testing evidence and an evaluation of the final solution.

conditions.value: 3–5 A3 pages or equivalent digital media pages; includes annotated user stories and wireframes, a functional website developed in GitHub Codespaces, and a 200–300 word evaluation of the solution against design criteria and user needs.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 8 students develop and modify creative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and evaluate alternative solutions against user stories and design criteria. Students acquire, interpret and model data with spreadsheets and represent data with integers and binary. They design and trace algorithms and implement them in a general-purpose programming language. Students select appropriate hardware for particular tasks, explain how data is transmitted and secured in networks, and identify cyber security threats. They select and use a range of digital tools efficiently and responsibly to create, locate and share content; and to plan, collaborate on and manage projects. Students manage their digital footprint.

moderation.value:
Internal moderation is conducted systematically to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Year 7–8 Digital Technologies achievement standard. This process includes:

*   **Standardisation:** Faculty review of the Guide to Making Judgements (GTMJ) and assessment parameters prior to the design phase to ensure a shared understanding of the evidence required for each performance level.
*   **Monitoring (Week 6):** Collaborative review of student wireframes and user stories to ensure consistency in formative feedback and alignment with design thinking requirements.
*   **Moderation Conferencing (Week 9):** Teachers meet to review student work samples at key grade boundaries (A, C, and E) to validate assessment decisions regarding user experience design and solution evaluation.
*   **Cross-marking:** Departmental cross-marking of a representative sample of final website projects to ensure the reliable and objective application of performance descriptors across the cohort.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students begin by investigating the significance of a digital presence for businesses within the Yeppoon and Capricorn Coast community. Through a series of comparative case studies, they explore how local entities, such as coastal cafés or regional tradespeople, utilise websites to communicate brand value and secure customer engagement. Lessons focus on identifying the distinct features of commercial sites, such as booking systems and service catalogues, contrasted against personal or social media-driven platforms.

resources.value: Projector for live site analysis, list of local Yeppoon business URLs, feature-comparison graphic organiser, digital design journal template.

theory.value: The theoretical focus is on the role of digital systems in supporting commercial objectives. Students learn to identify core website components including 'Call to Action' (CTA) elements, trust signals, and service-oriented information blocks. Explicit instruction covers how business goals—such as lead generation or information dissemination—influence the selection of digital features. Students examine the difference between static and interactive content and discuss how professional design contributes to business credibility in a competitive local market.

prac.value: Students conduct a competitive audit of three local business websites, using a structured criteria sheet to evaluate functionality and user engagement. They work in small groups to present a 'feature breakdown' of a successful Yeppoon-based site, highlighting specific elements that attract customers. Individually, students select a local business category (e.g., hospitality, retail, or trade) and define the primary purpose of their proposed digital solution, documenting their initial findings in a digital design journal.

assessment.value: Formative: Completion of the competitive audit table and the formal selection of a business focus with a justified purpose statement.

outlineTheme.value: Students investigate the role of digital presence for local businesses, such as Yeppoon-based cafés or tradespeople. They analyse how businesses use websites to communicate value and attract customers, identifying the key features that distinguish successful commercial sites from personal ones. Through case studies, students explore the relationship between business goals and digital functionality.

activities.teacherDoes: Explain that design criteria function as the quality assurance 'rules' for the project. Differentiate between functional requirements—what the system actually does (inputs, processes, outputs)—and non-functional requirements—how the system performs (quality attributes, usability, and constraints). keyTeachingExperiences.value: The teaching arc moves to visual communication and accessibility, where students explore the impact of colour theory, typography, and layout on user experience. They develop a visual style guide that ensures brand consistency while meeting the diverse accessibility needs of the community. Students investigate how specific design choices, such as high-contrast palettes and readable font pairings, can improve the inclusivity of a digital solution for the Yeppoon community.

resources.value: Adobe Express or Canva, WebAIM Contrast Checker, Google Fonts, WCAG 2.2 'At a Glance' guide, visual style guide templates.

theory.value: Students examine the core principles of visual hierarchy and the psychological impact of colour in branding, specifically focusing on how local businesses use visual cues to signal trust and industry (e.g., coastal blues for tourism or earthy tones for local trades). Explicit instruction is provided on the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), focusing on perceivable and understandable content. Students learn about the importance of sans-serif typography for digital legibility and the technical requirements for colour contrast ratios to support users with visual impairments.

prac.value: Students use digital design tools to create a formal visual style guide for their chosen business. This includes selecting a primary and secondary colour palette using hex codes, defining heading and body font families, and designing standardised button styles. They apply these styles to a mock-up of a 'Hero' section, ensuring the layout follows the F-pattern for readability. Students must use an online contrast checker to validate that their chosen colour combinations meet accessibility standards before finalising their guide.

activities.title: Colour Psychology Foundations
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the psychological triggers associated with colour in branding. Use the Keppel Bay Marina website as a model: demonstrate using the eyedropper tool to identify the primary 'trust-blue' hex code (#0047AB). Explain that these choices aren't just aesthetic; they are strategic decisions to align with industry expectations (e.g., professionalism, stability, or accessibility). Provide a worked example: 'If we were branding a local organic cafe, we would avoid bright, synthetic reds because they signal urgency, not the grounded, fresh energy we want.'

activities.questioning:
question: Why might a financial institution avoid using high-saturation neon colours in their logo?
expected: Neon colours suggest urgency, novelty, or disruption, which conflict with the need to signal stability, long-term trust, and fiscal conservatism.
question: If a brand targets an older demographic with visual impairments, why is high-contrast colour choice a mandatory design step?
expected: Ensuring a high contrast ratio between text and background is critical for legibility and WCAG compliance, ensuring information is perceivable by all users regardless of visual ability.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions for reference: Blue: Trust, calm, professional. Green: Growth, health, nature. Red: Urgency, passion, excitement. Yellow/Orange: Happiness, energy, friendliness. Colour Theory Terms: Hex Code (A six-digit representation of a colour used in HTML/CSS), Contrast Ratio (The difference in luminance between text and background), Palette (A curated selection of colours used in a design project).

activities.title: WCAG Basics
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) as the international benchmark for digital equity. Define the core tenets: 'Perceivable' and 'Understandable'. Model the use of the WebAIM Contrast Checker: 'Today, we are testing the contrast ratio of the St Brendan's College logo colours. Watch the ratio update as I adjust the background luminance—a ratio of 4.5:1 is our target to ensure text remains accessible for users with visual impairments.'

activities.visibleInstructions: Listen to the presentation on digital accessibility standards and complete the missing terms in the guided notes worksheet.
activities.questioning:
question: Why are sans-serif fonts prioritised for digital interface design?
expected: They possess uniform stroke widths that reduce visual distortion on screen resolutions, making them significantly more readable at smaller sizes.
question: What is the practical implication of a 4.5:1 contrast ratio requirement?
expected: It guarantees that text is sufficiently distinct from its background, ensuring that users with low vision or colour blindness can effectively perceive content.
activities.scaffolding: WCAG Definitions: Perceivable: Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive. Understandable: Information and the operation of the user interface must be understandable. Contrast Ratio: A measure of the difference in luminance between text and background.

To create an inclusive user experience, designers must ensure content is {{2}} by using clear typography. Furthermore, maintaining sufficient colour {{4}} between text and background elements ensures that all visual information remains {{5}} under the WCAG 2.2 standards.

activities.title: Contrast Validation
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the WebAIM Contrast Checker using the Capricorn Coast Visitor Information website as a test case. Explicitly show how to input Hex codes and interpret the WCAG AA requirement of 4.5:1 for normal text. Example: 'Inputting #FFFFFF text against #0056b3 background shows a contrast ratio of 7.24:1, which is a Pass for WCAG AA.'
activities.studentsDo: Access the WebAIM Contrast Checker. Select their chosen local business and test two distinct colour pairings (e.g., primary button text on background, footer text on background). Record results in the provided validation table. If a pairing fails, adjust the Hex code iteratively until a passing ratio is achieved.

question: What is the specific minimum contrast ratio required to meet WCAG AA standards for normal text?
expected: 4.5:1.
question: Why might a high-contrast design be necessary for users with visual impairments, such as colour blindness?
expected: It ensures that text remains legible against background elements by providing sufficient luminance contrast, preventing text from 'bleeding' into the background.
question: If your branding colours fail the test, what is a professional strategy to maintain brand identity while ensuring accessibility?
expected: Darken or lighten the text or background colours slightly, or add a subtle border/outline, ensuring the change remains within the brand's aesthetic palette.
activities.scaffolding: WCAG AA Standard: 4.5:1 for normal text (under 18pt/24px). Contrast Ratio: Measures the luminance difference between foreground and background. Hex Code: A six-digit, three-byte hexadecimal number used in HTML/CSS to represent colours.

Model the identification of a 'Call to Action' (CTA) button style, noting how consistent border-radius and padding settings contribute to cohesive UI/UX. Show an example of an 'F-pattern' layout and explain that style guides ensure designers maintain this visual hierarchy regardless of the page type.

expected: It is typically used for interactive elements like buttons, links, or hover states to provide clear visual cues for user action.
question: How does an 'F-pattern' layout influence where you place your primary brand logo or navigation elements?
expected: It places high-value content along the top and down the left side, where the human eye naturally begins its scanning process.

Students learn about User Interface (UI) patterns, such as navigation bars, grids, and cards, and how these structures support the user journey planned in Week 3. Instruction covers the use of annotations in wireframes to communicate functionality and responsive design principles, explaining how layouts must adapt from desktop monitors to mobile devices to meet the needs of customers on the move.

They then transition to a digital wireframing tool to create detailed structural blueprints for three essential pages: Home, Services/Products, and Contact. activities.title: Divergent Thinking Principles
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the 'Crazy 8s' rapid sketching method on the whiteboard. Clearly articulate that the objective is ideation volume, not aesthetic polish. Model three distinct layouts for a hypothetical 'Capricorn Coast Visitor Information' landing page, emphasizing varying placements for the Primary Call to Action (CTA) button, navigation density, and hero image framing. Example: 'In layout A, we prioritise visual hierarchy by centering the hero image; in layout B, we prioritise conversion by placing the booking CTA in the top-right navigation bar.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's model sketches. Record spatial arrangements in the workbook. Maintain a rapid pace, avoiding self-editing or over-critiquing during the ideation phase.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the three sketch examples provided on the board. Do not commence digital prototyping. Use the workbook space to record layout concepts focused on element placement (headers, buttons, images).
activities.questioning:
question: Why is it strategic to sketch low-fidelity layouts before initiating digital wireframing?
expected: To rapidly iterate and validate structural arrangements without investing significant time into high-fidelity detail.
question: How does divergent thinking assist in solving complex navigation problems?
expected: It allows designers to explore multiple UI variations, ensuring the most efficient user path is discovered before settling on a single design.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for Reference:
- Low-Fidelity Prototyping: Basic, structural sketches focusing on interface layout and information architecture rather than visual polish.
- Divergent Thinking: A design process used to generate a large volume of varied creative solutions to a specific problem.
- Call to Action (CTA): An instructional element, typically a button, designed to prompt an immediate response from the user (e.g., 'Book Now').
activities.eLearning: Project sketches using the document camera. No laptops required during this rapid sketching phase.
activities.transition: Transition students immediately to the 'Crazy 8s' timed sketching session.

workbookSpec.title: Rapid Layout Ideation: Divergent Thinking
workbookSpec.prompt: Using the 'Crazy 8s' method, sketch three distinct homepage layout variations for your chosen business.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Teacher note: Expect variations in grid structure. Variation 1 should highlight menu placement. Variation 2 should highlight hero image ratio. Variation 3 should highlight contrasting button placement and whitespace.

sections.label: Layout Variation 1: Navigation Focus
Layout Variation 2: Visual/Hero Focus
Layout Variation 3: CTA/Conversion Focus

activities.workbookMaterials: Sketching template section in student workbook.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: N/A - This is a divergent ideation task. Evaluate student work based on the variety of layout approaches shown rather than technical accuracy. Success criteria: Student demonstrates three distinct spatial arrangements rather than three identical layouts with minor variations.

activities.title: Rapid Sketching Session
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the rapid ideation process. Use the whiteboard to sketch a 'Z-pattern' layout, emphasising where the eye moves across the page. Explicitly demonstrate placing the 'Call to Action' (CTA) button in the 'hero' section of the first wireframe. Provide verbal constraints every three minutes to encourage divergent thinking: 'Shift the navigation to a hamburger menu,' 'Make the service list the focal point,' or 'Remove the hero image to prioritise text.' Ensure students understand that low-fidelity sketches are about structural hierarchy, not aesthetic detail.
activities.studentsDo: Generate three distinct homepage wireframe variations in the provided templates. Students will apply the 'Z-pattern' and 'F-pattern' scanning principles to structure their layouts, ensuring each variation prioritises the business's primary Call to Action.
activities.visibleInstructions: Create three rapid layout variations. Use basic geometric shapes for placeholders: rectangles for images/cards and circles for buttons. You must include labels for core components. Annotate your sketches to indicate which user story each layout is attempting to solve.
activities.questioning:
question: Which layout successfully guides the user's eye to the Call to Action button first?
expected: The layout utilising contrasting white space and a F-pattern reading flow is most effective for conversion.
question: How must the layout adapt when transitioning from desktop to mobile devices?
expected: Content blocks must stack vertically, navigation must collapse into a mobile-friendly menu, and clickable areas must remain accessible for touch inputs.
activities.scaffolding:
UI Pattern Guide: 
- Hero Section: Large visual/headline capturing value proposition. 
- Z-Pattern: Eye movement starting top-left, moving right, then diagonally to bottom-left. 
- CTA: High-contrast button designed to prompt immediate user action (e.g., 'Book Now', 'Enquire'). 
- Footer: Secondary navigation and copyright information.
activities.eLearning: Use the YouTube resource 'call to action website buttons convert visitors' to understand the placement principles before sketching.
activities.transition: Exchange workbooks with a peer for a 2-minute structural critique focusing on navigation clarity.

workbookSpec.title: Rapid Homepage Wireframe Templates
workbookSpec.prompt: Sketch three homepage variations based on your chosen business. Ensure structural hierarchy is clear.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Teacher Note: Look for the clear placement of the primary CTA. In Layout 1 (F-pattern), the CTA should be top-right or centre-hero. In Layout 2 (Z-pattern), the CTA should be at the terminal point of the eye path. In Layout 3 (Grid), the CTA should be prominent within the service cards. Annotations should specifically reference user stories developed in week 2 (e.g., 'CTA placed here for customer booking').

activities.workbookMaterials: Graphic sketching templates with UI element key.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: This is a generative task. Success is measured by the student's ability to demonstrate three distinct layout strategies (F-pattern, Z-pattern, and card-based grid) that explicitly incorporate the business's CTA and navigation structure as defined in the Week 2 brief.

activities.title: Peer Review and Selection
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through an evaluative cycle by modelling the comparison of a wireframe against the 'User Story' criteria from Week 2. Example modelling: 'When looking at my draft, I ask: Does the placement of the 'Contact Us' button reduce user friction? If the answer is 'no' because it is buried in the footer, I mark that criterion as incomplete.'
activities.studentsDo: Students conduct a self-assessment of their three sketches, using the checklist to verify alignment with their business objectives and UI design principles. They then select one design to carry forward for digital wireframing.
activities.visibleInstructions: Evaluate your three low-fidelity sketches against the checklist criteria. Tick the features that successfully address your specific user stories.
activities.questioning:
question: How does your chosen layout directly address the 'As a customer' user story you defined in Week 2?
expected: It prioritises the critical information in the 'hero' section, reducing the steps a user must take to find services.
question: Why did you eliminate the other two sketch variations during this review process?
expected: The other variations contained unnecessary clutter or failed to make the primary Call to Action (CTA) prominent enough for mobile users.
activities.scaffolding:
Design Criteria Checklist Definitions:
- Hero Section: The first area of a web page visible to the visitor.
- Above the Fold: Content visible without needing to scroll.
- CTA (Call to Action): A specific button or link designed to prompt an immediate response (e.g., 'Book Now', 'Enquire Today').
- Navigation Hierarchy: A clear, predictable structure allowing users to move between Home, Services, and Contact pages.
activities.eLearning: Use YouTube search terms: 'call to action website convert visitors' to reinforce the importance of button placement.
activities.transition: Secure all paper sketches; move to digital wireframing software (Figma or Balsamiq) to begin the structural implementation of the selected layout.

workbookSpec.title: Wireframe Evaluation Criteria
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate each of your three sketches against these standard UI effectiveness criteria. Select the layout with the highest number of successful ticks.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: A successful layout must exhibit 'above the fold' CTA placement, logical navigation, and adherence to the user stories established in Week 2.
items: Hero section clearly communicates the business identity
Primary Call to Action (CTA) button is placed above the fold
Navigation menu is simple and limited to 4–5 core links
Layout aligns with the 'As a user, I want to...' story from Week 2
Visual hierarchy draws the eye toward the primary goal
Contact information is easily accessible without scrolling

activities.teacherAnswerKey: The selected wireframe should meet a minimum of 5 out of 6 checklist criteria. If a student's best sketch meets fewer than 4, require a rapid 'iteration sketch' to refine placement before moving to digital wireframing software.

lessons.title: Digital Wireframing: Structure and Blueprint
lessons.learningGoal: Construct digital wireframes for three essential business website pages.

orientate.smartStart: Recall the difference between low-fidelity (sketches) and high-fidelity (finished design).
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can create digital wireframes that map out my website's structure

activities.title: UI Patterns and Wireframe Components
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that high-fidelity design requires low-fidelity blueprints to prevent 'design fatigue.' Model the creation of a wireframe on the whiteboard or projected software (Figma). Example: 'Look at the Keppel Bay Marina homepage. The primary goal is booking. See how the Hero section places the 'Book Now' button immediately in the user's eye path. We don't worry about the photo color here; we worry about the layout logic.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration, focusing on how functional elements (buttons, grids) are placed. Complete the provided annotation exercise by identifying the four core structural patterns in the sample wireframe.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Identify the labelled sections of the website wireframe.
2. In the space provided, describe the functional purpose of each element.
3. Ensure your labels match the professional UI terminology discussed.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do wireframes prioritise placement over visual aesthetics?
expected: To confirm structural flow and user journey efficiency without the distraction of colour or imagery.
question: How does a card grid structure support the user's scan path?
expected: It breaks content into digestible, scannable blocks, making information retrieval faster and less overwhelming.
activities.scaffolding:
Core UI Patterns:
1. Navigation Bar: Fixed container for site-wide links.
2. Hero Section: The top-most visual element containing the unique value proposition.
3. Card Grid: A series of containers used for grouping related content (services, news, products).
4. Footer: The bottom container housing secondary navigation, social links, and legal/contact details.
activities.eLearning: Project the Keppel Bay Marina website for reference. Search YouTube for 'call to action website convert visitors' if demonstrating conversion triggers.
activities.transition: Transition directly to the Figma workspace to begin initial layout drafting.

workbookSpec.title: Wireframe Structure Analysis
workbookSpec.prompt: Using the provided wireframe figure, identify and annotate the following components by writing the correct terminology next to each callout number:
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1: Navigation Bar; 2: Hero Section (with CTA); 3: Card Grid; 4: Footer.
workbookSpec.figureHint: A layout representing a standard responsive website: 1(Top), 2(Under Nav), 3(Middle), 4(Bottom).

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Navigation Bar: Primary access to core pages; 2. Hero Section: Displays core brand message and primary Call to Action (CTA); 3. Card Grid: Groups service options for quick user scanning; 4. Footer: Provides essential supplementary information and contact points.

activities.title: Constructing Page Blueprints
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how to map a layout onto the provided stencil. Use the projector to show the 'Home' page setup: place the navigation bar at the top, define a hero image area, and place a Call to Action (CTA) button clearly. Model annotating the wireframe: 'Add a note here to justify why the phone number is in the header—it reduces friction for mobile users.' Provide a worked example of grouping elements like the footer contact details.
activities.studentsDo: Use the provided wireframe stencils to draft the structure for their three key pages: Home, Services, and Contact. Students must translate their earlier rapid sketches into these formal layouts, ensuring they include navigation, main content regions, and a clear CTA button.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Label your three stencils: Home, Services, Contact. 2. Sketch the layout for each page based on your design criteria. 3. Annotate your wireframes to show where user stories (e.g., 'View services' or 'Get a quote') are addressed. 4. Ensure navigation is consistent across all three sheets.
activities.questioning:
question: Why should the navigation bar be consistent across all pages?
expected: To establish a predictable user journey and help the user navigate the site easily without getting lost.
question: If your wireframe has no clear 'Call to Action' area, what is the impact on the business?
expected: The website will fail to convert visitors into customers, as there is no clear instruction or pathway for them to take the next step.
activities.scaffolding: Navigation: Always at top/left; Hero Section: High-impact image/heading; Content Area: Grid-based layout for services or text; CTA: Button/Form; Footer: Contact links/Copyright. Reference your sitemap created in Week 3 for hierarchy.
activities.eLearning: Students are using physical stencils for initial structural mapping before digitisation. Monitor for appropriate UI element scale and placement.
activities.transition: Check that students have annotated their three pages. Move into independent work by digitising these stencils into the chosen software.

workbookSpec.title: Website Layout Blueprint
workbookSpec.prompt: Draw the page layout inside the browser chrome. Annotate where your specific user stories are addressed.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Header: Logo left, Nav items right. Hero: Large rectangular placeholder with 'Image' label. Content: 3-column grid for services. Footer: Social links and 'Contact' button.

activities.workbookMaterials: Wireframe stencil templates with browser chrome frame
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Assessment of wireframe accuracy: 1. Navigation is identical on all three pages (Home, Services, Contact). 2. CTA is placed above the fold (in the top half of the screen). 3. Annotations explicitly link design elements to a user story (e.g., 'Price list here meets As a customer I want to compare prices'). 4. Footer contains essential business contact info as per the business design criteria.

activities.title: Refining Layouts
activities.teacherDoes: Model the 'fold' concept on the whiteboard, drawing a line at one-third of the page height. Demonstrate how to verify a CTA button's prominence by squinting to see if it remains the primary focal point. Circulate to ensure students are justifying their layout decisions against user stories.
activities.studentsDo: Finalise the placement of UI elements (navigation, headings, image placeholders, CTA buttons) within the digital wireframes. Review the wireframes against the provided technical checklist to ensure industry-standard structural elements are present.
activities.visibleInstructions: Ensure your wireframes are completed. Use the digital checklist in your workbook to verify that all essential structural and responsive elements are positioned correctly before submitting for peer review.
activities.questioning:
question: What if a user accesses this site on a mobile phone instead of a desktop?
expected: The layout must be responsive; elements should stack vertically, and the navigation bar may need to collapse into a hamburger menu.
question: How do you evaluate if your Call to Action (CTA) is effectively prominent?
expected: It should be placed 'above the fold', use contrasting size or colour, and have enough white space around it to draw the user's eye.
activities.scaffolding:
Navigation & UI Standards: 
- Above the Fold: The area of the page visible without scrolling. 
- Responsive Grid: Elements aligned to a consistent column structure (e.g., 12-column grid). 
- Footer Anchors: Essential business information (Contact, Socials, Address).
activities.eLearning: Students should refer to the YouTube search terms 'call to action website convert visitors' to understand placement psychology if their CTA feels ineffective.
activities.transition: Save wireframes in the project folder and prepare for final self-reflection.

workbookSpec.title: Wireframe Structure Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify the following structural requirements are met for your Home, Services, and Contact page wireframes.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All items should be ticked 'Yes' as they represent the minimum viable product (MVP) design standards.
items: Primary navigation bar is consistent across all three pages.
Primary Call to Action (CTA) is located 'above the fold' on the Homepage.
Content blocks include descriptive placeholders (e.g., [Hero Image], [Service Title], [Price List]).
Footer contains essential contact information (e.g., Email, Phone, Social links).
Whitespace is provided between major sections to prevent clutter.
Responsive layout: Mobile stack order is identified or annotated.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: The checklist acts as a formative assessment tool. Students must tick 'Yes' for all items to proceed to the final review phase. If a student checks 'No', they must provide a brief annotation on the wireframe explaining why that element is missing or how it will be implemented in the high-fidelity design phase.

culminate.smartFinish: Self-check: List one aspect of your wireframe that might be hard to use on a small screen.
culminate.summarise: Summarised how wireframes act as the skeleton for the final design before adding content and code.
culminate.nextSteps: Annotating the wireframes with user stories in the next session.

lessons.title: Annotating for User Experience
lessons.learningGoal: Justify design choices by annotating wireframes with user story requirements.

orientate.smartStart: Recall the 'As a... I want... so that...' format from Week 2.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain how my design meets specific user needs

activities.title: Linking Criteria to Components
activities.teacherDoes: Define 'Design Rationale' as the cognitive process behind UI decisions. Model the annotation of a homepage element using the Keppel Bay Marina homepage. For example: 'Primary CTA button placed in the top-right navigation bar to ensure high visibility for mobile users, addressing User Story #1: Booking a berth quickly.' Emphasise that effective annotations create an explicit, traceable link between the business requirement and the user interface element.
activities.studentsDo: Analyse the provided homepage wireframe. Draft a formal rationale statement for their chosen Call to Action (CTA) component, ensuring it references a specific design criterion or user story.
activities.visibleInstructions: Draft a formal rationale statement explaining the strategic placement of your Call to Action (CTA) button. Reference your specific User Story in the justification.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must a design be 'functional' before it is 'aesthetic'?
expected: If a layout fails to support the user's primary goal, such as contacting the business or finding services, the visual design is rendered ineffective regardless of its stylistic quality.
question: What distinguishes a standard label from a design annotation?
expected: A label identifies what an element is, whereas an annotation explains the 'why'—justifying its position, behaviour, or necessity in relation to the project goals.
activities.scaffolding:
Design Rationale: The evidence-based justification for a design choice, explaining how a specific layout or element solves a user problem. 

Annotation Structure: 
1. Element identified (e.g., 'Hero Image'). 
2. Strategic decision (e.g., 'Placed above the fold'). 
3. Benefit/Requirement (e.g., 'Supports immediate brand recognition').
activities.eLearning: Refer to the Keppel Bay Marina homepage for examples of prominent navigation and clear conversion pathways.
activities.transition: Transition to the guided wireframe annotation activity, where students will apply these rationales to their own design drafts.

workbookSpec.title: Drafting Design Rationale
workbookSpec.prompt: Identify your primary Call to Action (CTA) component and justify its placement based on the user's journey. Ensure your rationale connects the component to your project requirements.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Component: 'Enquire Now' Button. Location: Top navigation bar. Rationale: Placing the primary conversion point in the persistent top navigation ensures accessibility from any page section, directly addressing the requirement for quick contact access as requested in User Story #3.

sections.label: Component Identifier
Proposed Location on Wireframe
Rationale (Justification of Design Choice)

activities.teacherAnswerKey: The rationale must explicitly link the component to a user story. A high-quality response will include: 1. Identification of the component. 2. A specific location (e.g., 'Above the fold' or 'Footer'). 3. A clear justification rooted in user behaviour (e.g., 'minimising cognitive load', 'reducing click-depth', or 'maintaining consistency with industry patterns'). Example: 'Navigation Menu: Placed at the top-centre. Rationale: Users anticipate navigational links here, reducing time-to-task completion for finding Service pages.'

activities.title: Annotating Wireframes
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that effective annotation acts as a 'contract' between your design choices and the user story requirements established in Week 2. Model the annotation process by projecting a wireframe section and demonstrating how to write a rationale: 'The Call to Action button is placed in the top-right header position to ensure immediate visibility for mobile users seeking quick conversion, directly satisfying the user story: As a customer, I want to book online.'
activities.studentsDo: Students will apply annotations to their wireframes. They must complete the mapping table to demonstrate how specific UI elements directly facilitate the user stories defined in their project proposal.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using your wireframe draft, complete the table below to map UI elements to your User Stories. Provide a specific design rationale for each choice, explaining how the placement addresses the user's needs.
activities.questioning:
question: How does your chosen layout for the contact form ensure users can find help without scrolling?
expected: Expected: Placing the contact form or link in the sticky header or footer ensures consistent access regardless of the user's scroll position, satisfying the 'I want to enquire' user story.
question: If a user story requires viewing pricing, why is a card grid layout preferable to a text list?
expected: Expected: Card grids allow for visual hierarchy and easy comparison, which is better for scanning, supporting the user's goal of identifying services quickly.
activities.scaffolding: Annotation Formula: [UI Element Name] | [User Story Addressed] | [Rationale: Why this placement/design choice helps the user]. Example: Search Bar | As a guest, I want to find specific info | Placed in header for immediate access from any page.
activities.eLearning: Use Figma wireframe files. Students should export their final annotated wireframes as PDFs for inclusion in their design portfolio.
activities.transition: Transition to final review checklist.

Row 2: Booking Button | As a customer, I want to book online | High-contrast colour and top-right placement to ensure the primary CTA is the first interaction point. Row 3: Footer Contact Info | As a potential client, I want to call the business | Placed in the footer with click-to-call link for mobile users.

activities.workbookMaterials: Table mapping wireframe items to design rationale
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. UI Element: Navigation Menu. User Story: As a visitor, I want to explore services. Rationale: Located in a sticky header to provide constant access during site exploration.
2. UI Element: Booking Button. User Story: As a customer, I want to book online. Rationale: High-contrast colour and top-right placement to ensure the primary CTA is the first interaction point for conversion.
3. UI Element: Footer Contact Info. User Story: As a potential client, I want to call the business. Rationale: Placed in the footer with click-to-call functionality, catering to mobile users who require immediate assistance.

activities.title: Reviewing against Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Facilitate a final peer-review session. Model how to check a wireframe against the 'Service/Product' user story by pointing to a specific annotation and asking: 'Does this label explain the interaction or just the visual appearance?'. Ensure students understand that annotations must be legible and precise for a developer or AI tool to interpret.
activities.studentsDo: Conduct a self-audit of their three wireframes using the checklist. Identify any missing annotations and add them using a red pen on paper or a comment layer in their wireframing tool.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the checklist below to verify the quality and completeness of your wireframe annotations. Ensure every critical user story from your Week 2 brief is represented by a specific annotation on your wireframe.
activities.questioning: How do these annotations bridge the gap between a design concept and a functional website? Expected: They explain the intended behavior and logic behind the static visuals. Why must we explicitly link annotations to user stories? Expected: To ensure every design element provides measurable value to the target user and prevents 'feature creep'.
activities.scaffolding: Annotations should address: 1. Target Audience interaction (e.g., 'Button opens contact form'). 2. Content placement (e.g., 'Hero image displays current seasonal offer'). 3. Responsive behaviour (e.g., 'Stack grid items for mobile view').

activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the 'CTC' framework: Context (Role/Setting), Task (The Objective), and Constraints (Rules/Boundaries). Model a prompt for the Keppel Bay Marina website: 'You are an expert web developer. Write HTML for a navigation header. Include a <nav> tag with 4 links: Home, Dining, Berthing, and Contact. Use semantic HTML5 only.' Demonstrate a 'poor' prompt vs. this 'CTC' prompt, showing how vague input leads to poor code. Direct students to the workbook anatomy diagram.

question: What happens to the HTML output if we omit the 'Constraints' section of the prompt?
expected: The AI might use outdated tags (like <div> instead of <nav>), fail to include the required links, or add unnecessary formatting, leading to non-semantic code.
question: Why is it essential to explicitly tell the AI 'You are an expert web developer'?
expected: This provides critical 'Context', setting the AI's persona and forcing it to default to professional, modern, and industry-standard coding conventions.
activities.scaffolding: Prompt Anatomy Framework: 1. Context (Role/Persona): Defines 'who' the AI is acting as (e.g., Senior Web Developer). 2. Constraints (Rules/Formatting): Defines 'how' it should be built (e.g., Must use semantic tags, CSS classes, or specific IDs).

activities.title: The Link to Style
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the standard HTML5 boilerplate structure in GitHub Codespaces. Model the 'Separation of Concerns' principle: HTML defines semantic structure within the <body>, while the <head> contains metadata and external references. Display the syntax for the <link> element. Example: '<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">'. Explain that the 'href' attribute acts as the file path locator for the browser. Emphasize that if this path fails to resolve, the browser defaults to browser-native styling, rendering the layout unstyled.
activities.studentsDo: Navigate to the project index.html file in their Codespace. Locate the <head> tag and insert the required link tag into the placeholder to establish the connection between the HTML document and their external style.css file.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is it best practice to place the link tag within the <head> element rather than the <body>?
expected: The <head> contains metadata and document configuration, ensuring the stylesheet is loaded and parsed before the visible content in the <body> is rendered, preventing a flash of unstyled content.
question: If you rename your CSS file to 'site-styles.css' but do not update your HTML, what technical outcome will occur?
expected: The browser will throw a 404 Not Found error for the CSS file, and the webpage will load without any applied CSS styles, appearing as plain HTML.
activities.scaffolding: Syntax definition: <link rel="[relationship]" href="[filepath]">. The 'rel' attribute defines the relationship between the current document and the linked document. The 'href' attribute specifies the URL or relative path of the linked resource.

activities.title: Vocabulary: The Box Model
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that every HTML element renders as a rectangular box. Define the three components of the Box Model: Margin (the outermost transparent space), Border (the visible edge), and Padding (the internal spacing between content and border). Demonstrate using Browser Developer Tools (Elements panel > Computed tab) to highlight how changing padding expands the background area, while margin pushes away adjacent elements. Model an example: 'If I add 20px of padding to a button, the visual footprint increases by 40px total due to the padding on both left and right sides.'

activities.questioning:
question: Why does adding padding impact the total computed width of a UI button?
expected: Padding adds space inside the border, which is added to the element's content width, effectively increasing the button's overall size on the page.
question: What is the primary difference between margin and padding in terms of background-color?
expected: The background-color property extends into the padding area, whereas the margin is transparent and sits outside the border.
activities.scaffolding: Margin: The transparent area outside the border; pushes elements away from neighbors. Border: The line or boundary surrounding the padding and content. Padding: The space between the content and the border; background colours apply here.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: In the final implementation phase, students move into structured testing and user trials to validate their digital solution. They engage in peer-testing cycles where they observe other students interacting with their website, looking for navigation bottlenecks or layout breaks. Students collect formal feedback based on their original user stories to determine if the prototype successfully meets the needs of the target audience. The week concludes with a final 'bug-fix' sprint, where students use their collected data to perform iterative improvements to the site's code and usability.

resources.value: Usability testing templates, screen recording tools, project submission portal, final design criteria checklist.

theory.value: The theory focuses on the 'Evaluation' and 'Testing' phases of the design cycle. Students learn about different testing methodologies, such as 'Think Aloud' protocols and usability checklists. Instruction covers how to categorize feedback into 'Critical Bugs' (functionality issues) and 'Enhancements' (aesthetic improvements). Students explore the importance of cross-browser and cross-device testing, understanding why a website might appear differently on a smartphone compared to a desktop monitor. They are also taught how to document these tests as evidence of an iterative design process.

prac.value: Students conduct a formal usability test with two peers, using a structured observation sheet to record how easily the users can find specific information (e.g., 'Find the business phone number' or 'Locate the price list'). They document any identified issues in a simple 'Bug Log'. Following the testing, students return to their code to fix high-priority issues, such as broken links or overlapping text on small screens. The final lessons are dedicated to polishing the code and preparing the design journal for the project submission.

assessment.value: Summative: Final submission of the 'Website Prototype' project, including the functional GitHub site, testing evidence, and the design documentation.

outlineTheme.value: In the testing phase, students conduct structured user trials to collect feedback on the website’s functionality, layout, and usability. They record evidence of bugs or navigation issues and use this data to perform iterative improvements to the prototype. This process ensures the final solution is robust and meets the needs of the identified target audience.

expected: It provides objective evidence of the user's cognitive load and navigation struggles, rather than relying on the designer's assumptions.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Usability: The effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction with which users achieve goals. Think Aloud: A method requiring users to verbalise thoughts while completing tasks. Bug: A failure of the system to perform a function as documented. activities.title: Modelling the 'Think Aloud'
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the 'Think Aloud' protocol: users must verbalise their thought process while navigating. Model this using the St Brendan's College website (https://www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au/). Ask a volunteer student to find the 'Term Dates'. Model the role of the observer: remain silent, record actions, and note verbal cues. Example script: 'I am looking for the calendar link in the navigation menu... I see Admissions but I am not sure if Term Dates are there... I am clicking here now.' Emphasise that as the observer, you do not intervene, even if the user is struggling, as this biases the data.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is it critical that the observer remains silent during a 'Think Aloud' session?
expected: The observer's goal is to test the intuitiveness of the design. If the observer provides hints or guidance, the data becomes biased and does not reflect a genuine user experience.
question: Beyond spoken words, what non-verbal cues indicate a usability bottleneck?
expected: Rapid scrolling, hovering over non-clickable elements, repeating clicks in the same area, or navigating back and forth between the same two pages.
activities.scaffolding:
Think Aloud Observation Guide:
1. Verbal Cues: Quotes of what the user is thinking/stating.
2. Navigation Path: The specific sequence of clicks taken.
3. Friction Points: Moments of hesitation, confusion, or incorrect clicking.

question: What does a 'horizontal scrollbar' appearing in a mobile preview indicate regarding your CSS implementation?
expected: It indicates a failure in responsive design, usually caused by an element having a fixed pixel width that exceeds the viewport width, or by block-level elements failing to inherit parent constraints.
question: If your hero image is scaling incorrectly, what specific CSS properties should you inspect to ensure it remains responsive?

activities.scaffolding:
Responsive Breakpoint Reference:
- Mobile (Portrait): 320px–480px. Check text readability and vertical stacking.
- Tablet: 768px–1024px. Check multi-column layout handling.
- Desktop: 1200px+. Check container alignment and whitespace.
- CSS Fix Strategy: Ensure 'meta viewport' tag is in HTML head; use percentage-based widths instead of fixed pixels; implement Media Queries (@media) for structural changes.

activities.title: Vocabulary of Maintenance
activities.teacherDoes:
Present the rationale for post-development maintenance. Discuss why developers must consider the 'lifecycle' of a digital product for a Yeppoon business like the Keppel Bay Marina or Capricorn Coast tourism operators. Explicitly define: 
1. Future-proofing: Designing a system to accommodate future updates without extensive redesign. 
2. Scalability: The system's capacity to handle increased traffic or content volume. 
3. Technical Debt: The long-term costs of selecting quick, suboptimal coding solutions over robust ones. 
4. Responsive Design: Ensuring seamless adaptability across various hardware. 
Model an example by explaining how a 'static' hard-coded menu creates 'Technical Debt' if the business needs to update it weekly.

expected: It increases their costs over time because they have to pay a developer to fix 'messy' code or rebuild parts of the site that should have been efficient from the start.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference: 
- Future-proofing: Proactive design strategies that anticipate future needs, reducing the need for costly redesigns.
- Scalability: The capability of a system to maintain performance levels while experiencing increased data, traffic, or feature additions.
- Technical Debt: A metaphorical term describing the 'cost' of additional rework caused by choosing easy, temporary solutions now rather than better, robust approaches.
- Responsive Design: A development approach that ensures website content adjusts fluidly to match the screen size and resolution of the device viewing it.

lessons.title: The Local Business Showcase
lessons.learningGoal: Present a functional website prototype and evaluate peer solutions using structured design criteria.

orientate.smartStart: Open your website prototype. Check that your Home page and at least one other page load correctly. Sit at the rear of your chair when ready.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can present my website and provide constructive feedback to my peers

activities.title: Presentation Etiquette and Rubric Review
activities.teacherDoes: Deliver a concise, professional 2-minute pitch for a mock Yeppoon business (e.g., Keppel Bay Marina). Model the language: 'This website addresses the [Business Name] need to [Core Goal]. I prioritised accessibility by implementing [Feature, e.g., semantic navigation], which directly supports our primary User Story.' Demonstrate the Peer Feedback Checklist, emphasising that 'constructive' feedback focuses on evidence-based observations rather than personal opinion. Model identifying a 'miss' (e.g., 'The navigation bar colour contrast is low') versus a 'hit' (e.g., 'The call-to-action button is highly visible').
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher pitch and annotate the Peer Feedback Checklist. Students map the teacher's verbal cues to the written checklist items to ensure they understand the evidence required to tick each box during the gallery walk.
activities.visibleInstructions: Listen to the demonstration pitch. As you hear the teacher address a criterion, tick that box on your checklist. Add one note in the margin about what 'evidence' looks like for that criterion (e.g., for 'Brand Identity' note: 'check for matching logo colours').
activities.questioning:
question: What distinguishes 'constructive' feedback from simple praise in a professional design context?
expected: Constructive feedback references specific project requirements or user stories, identifying both successes and actionable areas for technical improvement.
question: Why is it essential to explicitly state the 'User Story' when presenting a digital solution to a local business stakeholder?
expected: It validates the design decisions as functional and purposeful, demonstrating that the prototype solves a specific problem rather than just being aesthetically pleasing.
activities.scaffolding:
Pitch Template:
1. The Hook: 'This website is designed for [Business] to solve [Target User Problem].'
2. The Solution: 'My functional prototype streamlines this process by [Action].'
3. The Proof: 'As seen here, [Feature] ensures that [Result].'
4. Future-Proofing: 'I have structured the code to allow for easy updates to [Service/Menu].'

workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Teachers should look for students who can justify their ticks with specific references to the prototype's navigation or design elements. A 'checked' box requires the peer to demonstrate the feature functioning in real-time.

activities.title: The Showcase Gallery Walk
activities.teacherDoes: Model professional presentation etiquette: stand, make eye contact, and clearly articulate the 'why' behind design choices. Use the script: 'When pitching, explicitly mention one feature that meets your local business’s specific need and how you used AI to debug or generate that code. Reviewers, you must provide feedback that is specific—comment on both function and aesthetics.'
activities.studentsDo: Rotate through the gallery in pairs. Presenters explain their site functionality and design logic to two peer reviewers. Reviewers test navigation links and complete the required evaluation tables in their workbooks.
activities.visibleInstructions: Presenters: Deliver a concise 2-minute pitch covering design choices and AI utility. Reviewers: Navigate the site, test the CTA responsiveness, and document constructive feedback on technical and aesthetic performance.
activities.questioning:
question: Which peer website had the most effective Call to Action, and how did it prompt user engagement?
expected: A clear, high-contrast button that stands out against the hero image, with directive text like 'Book Now' or 'Contact Us'.
question: What common design patterns did you identify across multiple projects that enhance user experience?
expected: Consistent navigation bars, mobile-responsive layout adjustments, and use of whitespace to reduce cognitive load.
activities.scaffolding:
Evaluation Criteria: 
1. Functionality: All links lead to active pages; images load correctly.
2. Design: Contrast ratios are accessible; typography is consistent with the business branding.
3. Utility: The AI-generated code successfully solves the intended user problem.
Feedback Stems: 'Your use of [Component] effectively addresses [Business Need] because...'; 'A technical strength of your site is...'; 'To improve the user journey, you could...'
activities.eLearning: Use the 'call to action website buttons convert visitors' YouTube resource to remind students what to look for when evaluating effective web design.
activities.transition: Return to your own desk and synthesize the received feedback into a list of three final improvements to be made before the final project submission.

activities.title: Final Submission and Submission Checklist
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the 'Final Audit' protocol. Model the process of committing the final main branch to GitHub and ensuring public repository visibility. Instruct students to verify that their Design Journal (PDF/Doc) is attached to the final LMS submission. Remind students: 'Your submission acts as the source of truth for your assessment. Ensure your repository link is active and the documentation corresponds directly to the functional prototype demonstrated today.'
activities.studentsDo: Conduct a final repository commit. Verify their GitHub repository is public (if required) or accessible via the provided URL. Cross-reference their file naming conventions against the task sheet. Upload the digital Design Journal to the LMS.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Verify all code changes are pushed to the remote repository. 2. Ensure repository visibility is set to Public (or shared with the teacher). 3. Complete the 'Final Submission Checklist' in your workbook. 4. Upload your Design Journal to the LMS.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is it essential to verify the public accessibility of your GitHub repository link before submission?
expected: If the link is private or broken, the assessor cannot evaluate the functionality of the digital solution, resulting in an inability to grade the code.
question: How does your final evaluation table connect the original user stories to your completed code?
expected: It demonstrates a traceable path from user requirements to technical implementation, confirming the project meets the assessment standards.
activities.scaffolding: Submission Checklist: 1. GitHub Repository URL (Main Branch). 2. Digital Design Journal (includes: User Stories, Wireframes, Style Guide, Evaluation Table, Peer Feedback Summary). 3. Final code push complete (timestamp verification). 4. Code assets (CSS/Images) linked correctly in HTML.
